title: Greedy Best-First in Edinburgh: Find the Fastest Way!
description: Watch Greedy Best-First race across a real street-graph of Edinburgh (New Town), choosing routes using only a heuristic estimate to the goal. In this visualization, you’ll see how fast “best-looking” paths emerge—and why greedy choices can sometimes miss the absolute shortest route.
ig_caption:
🗺️✨ Greedy Best-First is sprinting through Edinburgh (New Town)!

In this visualization, the algorithm runs a **graph search** on a real street network (nodes = intersections, edges = road segments) and always expands the frontier node with the **lowest heuristic h(n)**—typically the estimated distance to the target (e.g., straight-line/Haversine distance).

🔍 **Deep intuition:** it’s like asking, “Which street *looks* closest to the destination?” at every step. That makes it *blazingly fast* in practice, but because it doesn’t prioritize full path cost (unlike A*), it may commit to a promising direction that later leads to detours.

⚙️ **What to look for in the animation:**
➡️ The frontier rapidly concentrates near the goal-facing corridor.
➡️ You can see heuristic-driven expansion waves across the street graph.
➡️ Compare the explored area vs. the final path to understand the greedy bias.

📣 Want more real-city algorithm reels? Comment the next city district you want (and whether you prefer shortest-path vs. fastest-found), and hit **follow** for more coding visuals! 🚀
fb_caption:
Ever wondered how a map turns into a computable puzzle? In this reel, **Greedy Best-First** solves pathfinding on a real street network: intersections become nodes, roads become edges, and the search expands the next node that *seems* closest to the goal using a heuristic estimate.

📌 Learn the mechanics of heuristic graph search—and then share this video with a friend who loves algorithms or navigation tech!
